A union of 27 European countries that share a single market, common laws in many fields and, for most of them, a single currency. It grew out of the rubble of the two world wars, from the idea that countries bound together by trade would not fight again.

  • 1951: six countries (France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) pooled their coal and steel.
  • 1957: the Treaty of Rome created the European Economic Community, a customs union. The Common Agricultural Policy followed in 1962.
  • 1993: the Maastricht Treaty turned the Community into the European Union.
  • 1999 to 2002: the euro replaced national currencies in most members.
  • 2004 and 2007: twelve countries joined, most of them former communist states such as Poland, Estonia and Romania. Croatia followed in 2013.
  • 2020: the United Kingdom left.

Students move between its universities through the Erasmus programme, and its anthem is the "Ode to Joy" from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012. Its hardest tests have included the debt crisis after 2008 and the migrant crisis of 2015.
